title: Tales in stone
hook: Jataka carvings at Bharhut and Borobudur, paintings on the cave walls at Ajanta

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maddi, searching all night for her children. Your line: Maddi's grief. Today, the tales leave the page.

A stone post, its faces carved with round panels. On one round panel, a deer kneels in front of a king. On another, monkeys cross a river on a bridge made of their own bodies. Next to some of the panels, a few letters are cut into the stone: the name of the tale. Somebody, long ago, wanted to make sure you knew which story you were looking at. This is the railing of a stupa at Bharhut, in India.
screen: `A CARVED STONE POST.` → `A DEER BEFORE A KING.` → `THE TALE'S NAME, CUT IN STONE.`

segments.voice: The carvers at Bharhut didn't only show the tales; on some panels they carved the tale's name beside the picture. So a scene of animals and kings isn't a guess. The stone tells you which birth story it is, and scholars can match it with the tales we still read. On the island of Java stands Borobudur, a huge Buddhist monument built in terraces, its galleries lined with carved panels, among them birth stories. Pilgrims walk around it, keeping the monument on their right, and the stories unfold beside them, scene after scene, climbing level by level. You read it with your feet. In western India, at Ajanta, halls were cut straight into a cliff, and their walls were painted with scenes from the Buddha's lives: a white elephant among lotus pools, a prince and his court, crowds and palaces, all on rock. Why put tales in stone at all? A carving teaches anyone who can see, whether or not they can read. A monk or a parent could stand at a panel and tell the story while pointing to it. And stone lasts. The tales we've been hearing were told aloud and copied, and also cut into rock and painted on walls in places far apart. The six-tusked elephant you met a few days ago stands on a railing at Bharhut and on a painted wall at Ajanta. When you hear a Jataka, you are hearing something people once walked past, touched and pointed at.
screen: `THE NAME CARVED BESIDE THE PICTURE.` · `READ WITH YOUR FEET.` · `PAINTED ON THE CAVE WALLS.` · `A TALE FOR ANYONE WHO CAN SEE.` · then, large: `THE TALES IN STONE.`

segments.voice: If you have a screen nearby, find a photograph of one panel from Bharhut, Borobudur or Ajanta and simply look at it: who is in it, and what moment did the carver choose? If you'd rather not look anything up, pick one tale from these weeks and picture it as a single carved scene, then close your eyes and rest with the breath.
Jataka. The birth stories carved and painted at Bharhut, Borobudur and Ajanta, for anyone who could see. Today's word.
Your line: the tales in stone. Stone kept the stories for people who never read them. That's day eight hundred forty-nine.

chat.says: Why would anyone carve Buddhist stories into stone railings and walls?
options: A carving teaches anyone who can see, even those who can't read, and it lasts.
Mostly as decoration; the carvings don't show any particular tale.
Because the tales were never written down anywhere at all.
chat.meaning: Carvings at Bharhut, Borobudur and Ajanta told the birth stories to anyone who could see, and some Bharhut panels carry the tale's name.

notes: No dates or counts given on purpose (claims rule). 'These weeks' refers to this app's own Block D (days 816–850), not to a historical claim.

Hook examples: the deer kneeling before a king and the monkey bridge (Mahakapi Jataka) are both known Bharhut subjects; confirm the deer scene (Ruru/Nigrodhamiga) and that both carry name labels or reword.
Ajanta: the white elephant among lotus pools refers to the Chaddanta (six-tusked elephant) paintings, and the prince and court to the Vessantara paintings; confirm.
Borobudur: Jataka and Jatakamala panels on the lower galleries; pilgrims circumambulate clockwise. Confirm the description 'among them birth stories'.
Fork answer is descriptive of Bharhut practice ('chose a key scene'); confirm. Original: जातक.
